damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (INT. MAIN ROOM) / Film Scene 7 (INT. ENTRANCE HALL) — Bellatrix summons Draco and nudges him forward
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 49-60: Narcissa calls Draco forward herself ('Draco, come here'). Draco approaches of his own volition under his mother's authority. His reluctance and fear are internal, navigated within the family dynamic. Lucius is the one consumed by excitement and ambition, contrasting sharply with Draco's paralysis.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bellatrix issues the command to fetch Draco ('Get Draco'), physically nudges him forward, and controls the scene. Draco enters 'from the shadows' and is managed by Bellatrix rather than by his own family dynamic. Lucius is diminished to a wine-glass-clutching bystander whom Bellatrix dismisses ('Pour yourself another glass of wine').
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book the Malfoy Manor identification scene is defined by the family triangle: Narcissa's cold authority, Lucius's desperate ambition, and Draco's terrified reluctance caught between them. The film transfers control of the scene entirely to Bellatrix. This flattens the intra-family tension that makes Draco's ambiguity so meaningful, and reduces the Malfoy family dynamic — a core element of Draco's arc — to a sideshow.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (INT. MAIN ROOM) — 'Call him, Draco' / Lucius calls the Dark Mark instead
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 94-96: Bellatrix orders 'Draco, pick them up!' (the wands) and 'Cissy, I think we ought to tie these little heroes up again.' No moment exists in the book where Draco is ordered to summon Voldemort; Bellatrix herself controls that threat. Draco's function in the scene is constrained refusal and silent non-identification.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bellatrix orders 'Call him, Draco.' Draco hesitates visibly — a moment of potential moral resistance — but then Lucius steps in and presses his own Dark Mark instead, bypassing Draco entirely. The film sets up Draco's hesitation as meaningful, then deflates it by having Lucius act.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film constructs a charged moment of Draco's possible refusal to summon Voldemort, which would be a significant moral beat, then immediately cancels it by transferring the action to Lucius. Draco's hesitation is teased as agency and then denied. This is doubly damaging: it invents a moment of apparent resistance that the book does not contain, then strips Draco of even that invented agency, leaving him as a passive, ambiguous non-actor rather than a character whose silent non-identification is his actual act of defiance.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 (INT. CORRIDOR TO MAIN ROOM) — Harry wrenches wands from Draco; Draco draws wand on Harry and Narcissa draws on doorway
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 91-99: During the escape, Draco fires jets of light alongside Narcissa and Greyback at Harry. He is an active participant in trying to stop the escape. The book is unambiguous: 'Jets of light flew from Draco's, Narcissa's, and Greyback's wands.' Draco actively opposes Harry here, consistent with his still-bound loyalty to Voldemort's side in this moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses and rearranges this: Narcissa and Draco draw wands after Harry Stupefies Lucius, jets of light spray, but the film quickly moves to Bellatrix's 'Stop or she dies' and Draco picking up wands on Bellatrix's order. The chandelier sequence has Draco screaming and covering his face (faithful), and Harry wrests wands from Draco. The film adds the line 'Call him, Draco' and Lucius pressing the Mark, restructuring Draco's role throughout.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor compression; the broad strokes of Draco's position in the escape scene survive, though some of the specific active resistance is blurred into the general chaos. Low standalone damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (INT. ROOM OF REQUIREMENT) — Draco confronts Harry, asks for his wand back, exchanges loaded dialogue
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 132-157: Draco confronts Harry backed by Crabbe and Goyle. His dialogue is brittle and impatient ('I virtually lived in the Room of Hidden Things all last year'). He repeatedly tries to restrain Crabbe from killing ('No!', 'STOP!', 'Don't kill him! DON'T KILL HIM!'). His motivation is to capture Harry alive for Voldemort. There is no moment in the book where Draco asks Harry why he didn't identify him at Malfoy Manor, nor any reflective dialogue about wand allegiance or unspoken debt.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Draco a lengthy, almost tender exchange with Harry. He asks for his wand back, explains 'It's my mother's... it doesn't understand me,' and Harry pointedly asks 'Why didn't you tell her? Bellatrix. You knew it was me. But you didn't say anything.' Draco fidgets and does not answer. This constructs an explicit, dialogue-driven acknowledgment of Draco's prior act of silent protection.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book keeps Draco's non-identification at Malfoy Manor as a silent, ambiguous act whose meaning is left to the reader. The film externalizes and sentimentalizes it into a quasi-intimate moment between Harry and Draco. While this isn't purely damaging — it does surface subtext — it over-explains Draco's internal conflict in a way that reduces his moral complexity to something more legible and less threatening. The brittle, status-conscious Draco of the books who 'virtually lived' in the Room of Requirement is softened into a conflicted almost-ally. Minor-to-moderate damage to the texture of his characterization.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 27 (EXT. COURTYARD) — Draco crosses to Voldemort's side; Narcissa hands him Harry's wand
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 186-187: 'I'm Draco Malfoy, I'm Draco, I'm on your side!' — Draco is on the upper landing pleading with a masked Death Eater, having already been trying to navigate to the Death Eater side. Ron punches him. 'And that's the second time we've saved your life tonight, you two-faced bastard!' In the book at the forest clearing (Scene 216), Lucius and Narcissa are 'running through the crowd, not even attempting to fight, screaming for their son' — the family is consumed by the search for Draco, not orchestrating his defection.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film stages a deliberate, public crossing: Lucius summons Draco with a nod, Narcissa calls him quietly ('Come, Draco'), and Draco walks across the courtyard in front of everyone, receiving Harry's wand from Narcissa. Ron mutters 'He saved your life' as Draco passes; Draco 'falters briefly, stung.' Voldemort praises him: 'Well done, Draco.' This is a choreographed, witnessed, morally weighted public defection scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most structurally damaging divergence in the corpus. The book has no such staged public crossing — the Malfoys at the forest clearing are desperately searching for their son, and Draco's ambiguous position throughout the battle is his most complex characterization. The film converts this ambiguity into a definitive, public act of betrayal against Harry, complete with Voldemort's approval and the crowd's baleful glances. It then immediately undercuts it with Ron's 'He saved your life,' but the damage is done: the film forces Draco into an unambiguous villain position at the climax, then asks the audience to simultaneously credit him with heroism. The book's Draco never has to make this public choice — his arc ends in moral suspension, which is thematically richer. The film's staging actively damages the audience's understanding of where Draco's arc lands.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (INT. ROOM OF REQUIREMENT) — Goyle (not Crabbe) sets the fire; Blaise replaces Goyle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 132-175: Crabbe and Goyle accompany Draco. Crabbe is the one who casts the Fiendfyre ('It's not normal fire; Crabbe had used a curse of which Harry had no knowledge'). Crabbe dies in the fire. Goyle is rescued unconscious by Ron and Hermione. This is a significant character beat: Crabbe, Draco's long-time lackey, defies him ('I don't take your orders no more, Draco. You an' your dad are finished') and dies for it.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Crabbe is replaced by Blaise Zabini; Goyle sets the fire and apparently dies in it ('the flames devour Goyle'). Blaise simply scarpers after being disarmed. The defiant 'You an' your dad are finished' line and the insubordination dynamic is absent from the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Crabbe's defection and death is a pointed punctuation on Draco's loss of status and power — his own enforcer turns on him and pays with his life. The film's substitution (likely due to the actor's real-world circumstances) loses this specific beat: the moment where Draco's social hierarchy collapses entirely around him, leaving him literally powerless and dependent on Harry. Goyle dying instead is emotionally flatter and removes the explicit 'your dad are finished' repudiation of Draco's authority.

main_damage_causes: Transfer of scene control from the Malfoy family dynamic to Bellatrix at Malfoy Manor, weakening the intra-family tension that drives Draco's arc
Invention and then cancellation of Draco's agency (the 'Call him, Draco' / Lucius presses the Mark sequence), leaving him as a passive non-actor at a moment designed to feel decisive
The staged public crossing to Voldemort's side in the courtyard, which collapses Draco's book-ending moral ambiguity into an explicit, witnessed act of betrayal that the book never stages
